name: Paul Graham lens
lens: Strategy seen from the founder's side of the table: growth as the definition of a startup, users over cleverness, small teams doing unscalable things early, and a bias toward making something people actually want.

principles.gist: A startup is a company designed to grow fast; growth rate, not age or technology or funding, is what makes it one.
principles.verbatim: A startup is a company designed to grow fast.
principles.implication: Judge an initiative by its effect on growth rate. A project that improves margin without improving growth is a different decision than it looks.

principles.gist: Early on, users need manual, unscalable attention. Founders who wait for the product to sell itself usually wait forever.
principles.verbatim: One of the most common types of advice we give at Y Combinator is to do things that don't scale.
principles.implication: A scalable-looking plan executed before demand exists is a plan to learn nothing. Budget for unscalable effort first.

principles.gist: Release early means releasing something minimal, not something broken. Minimal scope, working core.
principles.verbatim: By "release early" I don't mean you should release something full of bugs, but that you should release something minimal.
principles.essay: The Hardest Lessons for Startups to Learn
principles.implication: Cut scope, not quality. A smaller thing that works teaches you more than a large thing that is nearly ready.

principles.gist: The people are the most important ingredient; don't compromise on them to save time or money.
principles.verbatim: The people are the most important ingredient in a startup, so don't compromise there.
principles.implication: Cheap hiring is expensive twice: once in salary saved, and again in the cost of the wrong person owning a decision.

principles.gist: Statistically the most reliable way to avoid failure is to commit fully. Most founders of failed startups kept their day jobs; most successful ones did not.
principles.verbatim: Most founders of failed startups don't quit their day jobs, and most founders of successful ones do.
principles.implication: Partial commitment produces partial learning. If a venture is worth testing, test it at a commitment level that can actually succeed.

principles.gist: Makers work in half-day blocks and managers work in hours. Meetings fragment a maker's day into unusable pieces.
principles.verbatim: The mere consciousness of an engagement will sometimes worry a whole day.
principles.implication: Protect long blocks for the work that creates value. A calendar full of short commitments is an expensive way to feel productive.

principles.gist: Great opportunities hide behind work that looks unpleasant. People avoid the schlep and so never see the opportunity.
principles.verbatim: You should never shrink from it if it's on the path to something great.
principles.implication: When an opportunity looks unglamorous and everyone is ignoring it, the reluctance is often the moat.

principles.gist: Ideas come from problems, ideally your own. Trying to think of ideas directly produces plausible-sounding things nobody wants.
principles.verbatim: The way to get startup ideas is not to try to think of startup ideas. It's to look for problems, preferably problems you have yourself.
principles.implication: Ask what is broken in the business, not what product could be launched. The problem is the specification.

principles.gist: What you think about in the shower sets the ceiling on how good the work can be. Ambient worries crowd out the real problem.
principles.verbatim: It's hard to do a really good job on anything you don't think about in the shower.
principles.essay: The Top Idea in Your Mind
principles.implication: If the same unresolved question keeps surfacing unprompted, that is the real work. If nothing surfaces, the real work is being crowded out.

principles.gist: Returns to performance are superlinear. Being twice as good does not mean twice the customers; it means far more.
principles.verbatim: If your product is only half as good as your competitor's, you don't get half as many customers.
principles.implication: Marginal quality improvements near the top of a market are worth far more than the same effort spent broadening. Choose where to be best.

principles.gist: Very few of the most successful people are mean. Being disagreeable is not the same as being effective.
principles.verbatim: It struck me recently how few of the most successful people I know are mean.
principles.implication: Treat abrasiveness as a risk factor, not a proxy for rigour. The people who stay are the ones others choose to keep working with.

principles.gist: The more of your identity a belief occupies, the less able you are to reason about it. Politics and religion are uniquely useless to discuss for this reason.
principles.verbatim: People can never have a fruitful argument about something that's part of their identity.
principles.implication: When a strategy debate turns into a defence of who someone is, it has stopped being a debate. Separate the position from the person early.

principles.gist: The quality that predicts a good founder, compressed to two words. Its opposite is hapless.
principles.verbatim: A couple days ago I finally got being a good startup founder down to two words: relentlessly resourceful.
principles.implication: Look for evidence of finding a way around obstacles, not credentials. The trait is observable in past behaviour, not in interviews.

principles.gist: Confidence should rise with how often a belief has survived change. Most things change, so most confident opinions are stale.
principles.verbatim: If the world were static, we could have monotonically increasing confidence in our beliefs.
principles.essay: How to Be an Expert in a Changing World
principles.implication: Ask when a belief was last tested, not how strongly it is held. An opinion inherited from a stable era is a liability in a changing one.

principles.gist: Effectively all the returns in early-stage investing are concentrated in a few outcomes. Averaging across many small bets misreads the distribution.
principles.verbatim: Effectively all the returns are concentrated in a few.
principles.implication: If outcomes are power-law distributed, the mean is a misleading summary. Judge by the best case you can reach, not by the average of a portfolio you don't have.

principles.gist: Determination predicts success more reliably than intelligence. Investors spend more time on it than on ideas.
principles.verbatim: Like all investors, we spend a lot of time trying to learn how to predict which startups will succeed.
principles.implication: When choosing between a clever plan and a determined team, weight the team. Plans are cheap to change; persistence is not.

principles.gist: Smart people produce bad ideas because they optimise for cleverness and novelty rather than for a real problem.
principles.verbatim: Most of them had never seen the Web before we came to tell them why they should be on it.
principles.essay: Why Smart People Have Bad Ideas
principles.implication: Cleverness is a liability when it outruns contact with the customer. Test the idea against someone who has the problem.

principles.gist: To do something well you have to like it. Most successful people like what they do.
principles.verbatim: To do something well you have to like it.
principles.essay: How to Do What You Love
principles.implication: Sustained quality is hard to fake without interest. The work someone returns to voluntarily is where their best output will be.

principles.gist: Good procrastination defers errands to protect blocks for real work. Real work needs big chunks of time and the right mood; errands need neither.
principles.verbatim: Real work needs two things errands don't: big chunks of time, and the right mood.
principles.implication: Busy-ness is the most respectable form of avoidance. Protect the block; the errands will still be there.

principles.gist: Outsiders see what insiders cannot, partly because insiders learned the rules from the people who benefit from them.
principles.verbatim: Don't learn things from teachers of the thing.
principles.implication: The industry's consensus is a description of the industry, not of the opportunity. Treat best practice as evidence about incumbents.

principles.gist: People do great work for free when the audience and the collaboration are real. Business has something to learn from that motivation.
principles.verbatim: People have always been willing to do great work for free, but before the Web it was harder to reach an audience or collaborate on projects.
principles.essay: What Business Can Learn from Open Source
principles.implication: Motivation is cheaper than compensation when the work is visible and the collaboration is genuine. Pay is not the only lever on output.

principles.gist: Founders should stay close to the details and resist delegating to professional managers who optimise for not being blamed.
principles.verbatim: Founders should do things that don't scale, and stay involved in the details.
principles.implication: Management layers can quietly convert a company's edge into process. Watch for decisions being made by people with no exposure to the customer.

principles.gist: The future is already here in pockets. Find what is true somewhere but not yet everywhere.
principles.verbatim: The future is already here, it's just unevenly distributed.
principles.implication: Look for behaviour that already exists in a niche and is about to become general. The evidence precedes the trend.

principles.gist: Institutions that seemed permanent were products of a particular era and are now fragmenting.
principles.verbatim: The Refragmentation
principles.implication: Ask which of the business's assumed structures are era-specific. What looked like a law of nature may be a phase.

principles.gist: Wealth is made by making things people want, at scale, with leverage. Startups compress a working life into a few years.
principles.verbatim: The way to create the most wealth is to focus more on their needs than your interests.
principles.implication: Value capture follows value creation. A pricing decision that ignores what the customer gets is a decision to lose the customer.

principles.gist: Start small, aim for simple solutions even though they look less impressive, and deliver informally to avoid the cost of looking impressive.
principles.verbatim: If you deliver solutions informally, you save all the effort you would have had to expend to make them look impressive.
principles.essay: Six Principles for Making New Things
principles.implication: Polish is a cost with a return that is often zero. Spend it only where the customer sees it.

principles.gist: Great work across fields shares techniques: work on what you're curious about, aim to be the best, and iterate.
principles.verbatim: If you don't try to be the best, you won't even be good.
principles.implication: Ambition is a forcing function on quality. A team aiming at mediocrity will not reliably reach it either.

limits: Graham writes about startups seeking high growth. A stable, profitable small business is not his subject, and applying growth-maximising advice to one can destroy it.
The essays are drawn from Y Combinator's experience, which selects for a particular kind of company. The base rate he observes is not the base rate of all businesses.
Several principles are about founder psychology rather than business mechanics. They are useful as a lens on people, not as an operating model.
The corpus spans 2004-2024. Advice about fundraising and markets in the 2000s may be stale; the principles about users and focus age better.
He is an investor writing partly to promote investing. Where an essay argues for taking venture funding, read it as an argument from a party with an interest.
